Trail Physics · Unit 3: Forces & Cornering · Module 9

Uniform Circular Motion

Turning: arc length, angular velocity, centripetal acceleration and force, and how a banked turn helps.

Lesson coming

The question

Why does a wider line through a berm let you carry more speed?

The physics

  • Circular motion
  • Arc length and angular displacement
  • Angular velocity
  • Radius of curvature
  • Centripetal acceleration and force
  • Banking angles

The math

  • a_c = v² / r
  • F_c = mv² / r
  • ω = v / r
  • matched bank angle: tan β = v² / (rg)

About the model: Berm Lab uses an idealized steady banked-turn model. Its grip numbers are illustrative, not riding advice.

Learning objectives

  • Relate arc length, angle and radius
  • Relate angular velocity, speed and radius with ω = v/r
  • Calculate centripetal acceleration with a = v²/r
  • Calculate the inward force a turn needs and identify what supplies it
  • Explain how speed and radius change the demands of a corner
  • Explain how a banked turn supplies inward force, and find the matched bank angle

Helps to know first: Friction, Slopes and Springs.

The mountain biking connection

Every corner is a piece of a circle. To turn, a rider needs an inward force, from tire friction and from the tilt of a berm, and how much depends on speed squared over the radius of the line.

Learning activities

Interactive lab

Berm Lab

Pick a tight, middle or wide line, set your speed and bank the berm, then watch the forces, lean and grip demand of a corner change.
